name: Pandan
tagline: The green, sweet smell of Nyonya kaya and kueh.
story: Pandan is the defining aroma of Malay and Peranakan sweets: kueh, green Nyonya kaya, and the leaves wrapped around Nyonya rice dumplings.
When fruit for jam was hard to find, Hainanese and Peranakan cooks made kaya from coconut milk, eggs and pandan leaves instead. That's the kaya on your toast today.

sources.title: BiblioAsia: The Evolution of Chinese Food in Singapore

everyday.text: Pandan chiffon cake is the green, cloud-light cake of every Singapore bakery. The earliest local newspaper mention is a 1972 review of Bali Café.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Pandan

everyday.text: Pandan chicken is marinated chicken wrapped in the leaves and fried, so the smell cooks right into it.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Pandan

everyday.text: Many Singaporeans tuck fresh pandan leaves into cars and cupboards to keep cockroaches away. Pest experts say fresh leaves only mildly repel them, and dried ones can turn into food.

src.title: Rentokil Singapore: is pandan a cockroach repellent?

name: Jasmine
tagline: The flower of Little India's garland stalls.
story: Jasmine is one of the main fragrant flowers in Hindu garland-making, alongside rose, tuberose and chrysanthemum.
Garland makers have worked Little India's five-foot-ways for decades. Jothi Store & Flower Shop began in the early 1960s as a small stall selling garlands, betel leaves and prayer items.

everyday.text: Garlands come out for Pongal and Deepavali, for Thaipusam processions, and to bless a new home, car or shop.

everyday.text: Across South India and its diaspora, women string jasmine into their hair for festivals and offer it to the gods.

name: Nutmeg & mace
tagline: The spice that named Orchard Road.
story: One tree gives two spices: nutmeg is the seed, and mace is the red, lacy covering around it.

Raffles sent nutmeg seeds and saplings from Bencoolen in Sumatra. In the 1830s and 1840s, European residents turned old gambier estates around Orchard Road into nutmeg orchards, which are believed to have given the road its name. A disease wiped out the trees in 1857.

sources.title: NHB Roots: Orchard Heritage Trail
BiblioAsia: From Gambier to Pepper

everyday.text: Nutmeg trees still grow in the Singapore Botanic Gardens, some of them listed on NParks' Heritage Tree Register.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Nutmeg

everyday.text: In traditional remedies, nutmeg has been used for rheumatism and an upset stomach.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Nutmeg

name: Clove
tagline: Raffles' bet on the spice trade.
story: In 1822, Raffles set up Singapore's first botanical and experimental garden on Fort Canning Hill to grow cash crops, mainly nutmeg and clove.
At one point it held over 600 nutmeg trees and 300 clove plants. The garden closed in 1829, but a replica Spice Garden grows on the same slopes today.

sources.title: NParks: Fort Canning Park special features

everyday.text: Biting on a clove is an old toothache remedy. Its oil, mostly eugenol, numbs pain, which is why clove still turns up in toothpaste.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Clove

everyday.text: Cloves were also used to freshen linens and clothes, and next door in Indonesia they scent kretek cigarettes.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Clove

everyday.text: NParks runs free guided tours of the Fort Canning Spice Garden, where you can smell clove and nutmeg on the tree.

src.title: NParks: Spice Garden tour

name: Black pepper (& gambier)
story: Gambier and pepper were grown together, mostly by Teochew planters, and were already on the island when the British arrived in 1819.

By the late 1840s there were some 400 to 600 gambier and pepper plantations, and they drove large-scale clearing of Singapore's forests. Gambier itself was used for tanning, not perfume. Pepper is the note that carries the story.

sources.title: NLB Infopedia: Gambier
BiblioAsia: Deforestation in 19th-century Singapore

everyday.text: Pepper is the soul of Teochew bak kut teh: a clear pork-rib soup seasoned only with garlic, soy sauce and pepper.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Bak kut teh

everyday.text: Kai Juan Bak Kut Teh on the Balestier food trail has served the clear, peppery Teochew style for about 50 years.

name: Orchid
tagline: A hybrid national flower for a hybrid nation.
story: Agnes Joaquim, an Armenian Singaporean, bred the Vanda Miss Joaquim in her Tanjong Pagar garden, and it was described in 1893. It became Singapore's national flower on 15 April 1981. Singapore is the only country with a hybrid as its national flower.
Most orchids are only faintly scented, so an orchid note in perfume is an accord: an impression the perfumer builds from other materials.

sources.title: NParks: Vanda Miss Joaquim
BiblioAsia: Blooming Lies

everyday.text: Orchid diplomacy: since 1956, Singapore has named orchid hybrids after visiting leaders and guests. The first was Aranthera Anne Black; there are now more than 280.

everyday.text: The VIP orchids grow in the VIP Orchid Garden at the National Orchid Garden, inside the Botanic Gardens.

everyday.text: Orchids are the garland flower for secular events, chosen for their colour and their almost neutral scent.

name: Agarwood (oud) & sandalwood
local: gaharu · cendana · 沉香 · 檀香
tagline: The woods of mosque, temple and shophouse.
story: Malay and Muslim: minyak attar, an alcohol-free perfume oil, is listed as Singapore intangible cultural heritage, and agarwood is a key ingredient. Kampong Gelam became the trade's centre because of Sultan Mosque, where worshippers put on attar before prayers.
Chinese: joss-stick burning spread with 19th-century Chinese migration. Temple incense is often made with sandalwood or agarwood.

sources.title: NHB Roots: Minyak Attar
NHB Roots: Making of Joss Sticks

everyday.text: Muslims in Singapore still burn agarwood chips as incense at religious gatherings, such as Ramadan prayers in the lead-up to Hari Raya Haji.

src.title: NHB Roots: Minyak Attar

everyday.text: During the seventh lunar month, joss sticks, paper offerings and food appear along pavements and void decks to feed wandering spirits.

src.title: NHB Roots: Zhong Yuan Jie (Hungry Ghost Festival)

lore.text: The Hungry Ghost Festival rests on the belief that spirits without descendants to make offerings to them go hungry, so believers burn incense and paper for them.

name: Aquatic ginger
tagline: A beach-and-swamp ginger brought back from the brink.
story: A native ginger of sandy beaches and swamp forests, with small white to pale pink flowers. It's Critically Endangered in Singapore; in the wild it's recorded on Pulau Semakau.

NParks has salvaged it and replanted it along some Nature Ways, the planted streets that link up green spaces. You can see it at HortPark, Kent Ridge Park and the Botanic Gardens' Ginger Garden. One of the six batik-motif flowers in Singapore Airlines' Batik Flora.

name: Common dianella
tagline: Looks like wild grass, until the blue berries show up.
story: A tough native herb with sword-shaped leaves (that's what ensifolia means). It grows from Labrador Park's rocky shore to Chek Jawa, Kent Ridge and St John's Island.

Its flowers are tiny, white to bluish, and open in the afternoon. Then come shiny deep-blue berries, which birds eat; they're thought to be toxic to people. One of the six batik-motif flowers in Singapore Airlines' Batik Flora.

everyday.text: In the region its roots have gone into cosmetics and perfume, and its boiled leaves into incense.

lore.text: The genus is named after Diana, the Roman goddess of the wild.

name: Seashore purslane
tagline: A salty succulent that creeps along the shore.
story: A creeping succulent with fleshy leaves that grows on salty, sandy and muddy ground by the sea. In Malay it's gelang laut or gelang pasir.

In Singapore you'll find it on Pulau Ubin, Pulau Tekong, Pulau Semakau and at the end of Lim Chu Kang Road. Its small star-shaped flowers are green outside and pink inside. One of the six batik-motif flowers in Singapore Airlines' Batik Flora.

everyday.text: Around the world it's eaten as a sea vegetable, raw, pickled or cooked.

name: Simpoh lak
tagline: Big yellow flowers that last a single day.
story: A riverside tree up to about 25 m tall, with bright yellow flowers 8 to 10 cm across around a dark red centre. Each flower opens early in the morning and drops its petals by evening.
One honest note: Singapore Airlines calls all six batik flowers native, but NParks lists simpoh lak as non-native to Singapore. Its home range is Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Dillenia excelsa
SilverKris: SIA's five senses

everyday.text: The flowers are full of nectar and mostly worked by giant honey bees.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Dillenia excelsa

everyday.text: Another native, the simpoh air, has leaves so big that hawkers once wrapped tempeh and rojak in them, before plastic bags took over.

src.title: NParks: Simpoh Air

lore.text: Its cut branches root so easily that fences built from them have sprouted back into trees.

name: Utania nervosa
tagline: A rare tree botanists mislabelled for half a century.
story: A small native tree, usually 1 to 5 m tall, with hanging clusters of cream-yellow to white flowers. It's listed as Vulnerable in Singapore and has no common English name.
In 1962 it was misidentified as Fagraea racemosa. It wasn't sorted out until a 2014 revision of the genus. One of the six batik-motif flowers in Singapore Airlines' Batik Flora.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Utania nervosa

everyday.text: It belongs to the same plant family as the tembusu, the tree on the back of the $5 note.

name: White kopsia
tagline: Red and white, like the flag.
story: White petals around a red throat: the colours of Singapore's flag. It was named Kopsia singapurensis in 1923, decades before the flag existed. Its five petals are fused at the base, which NParks jokes makes them 'united'.

It's fragrant, each flower lasts a day, and in the wild here it grows only in Nee Soon Swamp Forest. It's Critically Endangered in Singapore and found nowhere else but Peninsular Malaysia. One of the six batik-motif flowers in Singapore Airlines' Batik Flora.

lore.text: In 1964 a kopsia was used in place of a ribbon to open the rebuilt herbarium at the Singapore Botanic Gardens.

name: Kopi & teh
tagline: The smell of a Nanyang breakfast.
story: Between the 1920s and 1950s, Hainanese coffeeshop owners popularised kopitiam culture and the Nanyang breakfast: kopi, teh, soft-boiled eggs and kaya toast. Teh is usually made with Ceylon tea.
Nanyang means 'South Sea' in Mandarin and refers to Southeast Asia. Nanyang-style kopi is traditionally made from Robusta beans roasted with sugar and margarine, then strained through a cloth 'sock'.

sources.title: NHB Roots: Traditional Breakfast of Kaya and Kopi
MICHELIN Guide: The Singaporean breakfast

everyday.text: Kopitiam code: kopi comes with condensed milk, O means no milk, C means evaporated milk, kosong means no sugar, siew dai less sugar, peng iced.

everyday.text: Teh tarik, pulled tea, was first sold by Indian-Muslim drink stalls after World War II. It is poured back and forth between two cups until it froths, ideally further than arm's length.

src.title: NHB: Teh tarik photo story

everyday.text: It's also called a mamak drink, from the Tamil word for uncle.

name: Calamansi
tagline: The small lime on every hawker plate.
story: Calamansi, called limau kasturi in Malay, is the small lime squeezed over dishes at Singapore's hawker centres, from Hokkien mee to Malay noodles and sambal belacan.
The plant first came from the Philippines, where it is still mostly grown. NParks lists it under both names, along with 'musk lime' and 'golden lime'.

everyday.text: Citrus plants like kumquat and four-season lime crowd doorways at Chinese New Year. Kumquat's Cantonese name, gam gat, sounds like 'gold and luck'.

name: Frangipani
tagline: The graveyard flower, and a perfumer's name.
story: NParks lists the white frangipani as the 'Singapore graveyard flower'. Its Malay names include kemboja and bunga kubur, 'grave flower'. Indian and Malay Muslims and Buddhists often plant it in cemeteries. Some Malay Muslims see its fallen morning flowers as an offering to the dead, and Hindus sometimes plant it near temples.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Plumeria obtusa

lore.text: In Malay folklore, the pontianak, the ghost of a woman who died in childbirth, gives off a strong smell of frangipani when she is near.

src.title: Wikipedia: Ghosts in Malay culture

lore.text: The flower was named after a perfume: a 17th-century almond glove scent made by the Marquis Muzio Frangipani. Its smell reminded botanists of his perfume.

src.title: JSTOR Daily: Plant of the month, frangipani

name: Torch ginger
tagline: The pink bud that perfumes rojak and laksa.
story: Torch ginger, bunga kantan, is grown for its aromatic young flower buds, which taste floral and tangy. NParks calls them a key ingredient in Chinese rojak and Penang asam laksa.
It grows in the Fort Canning Spice Garden today, next to the nutmeg and clove.
